chapter_theme: Neelakesi goes to Hastinapura to the Sankhya teacher Parasaran, draws out his twenty-five principles and his doctrine of a soul that does nothing yet experiences, then attacks it: a non-acting soul could not teach, speak, enjoy, be bound or be carried between births, and his defence of a second, acting soul destroys his own thesis.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Sankhya teacher of Hastinapura who has planted a challenge flag
the Ajivika teacher Neelakesi has just defeated, who directs her to the Sankhya

730.reading: When the defeated Ajivika had told her of him, Neelakesi went to Hastinapura to confront the Sankhya teacher who had planted a tall challenge flag there and was held by everyone as their authority.
730.nuance: ஆங்கவன் சொல்ல picks up the end of the Ajivika sarukkam (729), where she sends Puranan away; the flag planted to dare all comers (கொடி நட்டு) is the formal opening of a debate. எவர்க்கும் மறை என்று இருந்த is read here as 'regarded by all as their scripture or authority'; it could also mean he was hidden from or closed to everyone.
730.event: On Puranan's word Neelakesi goes to Hastinapura to meet the Sankhya teacher who has planted a challenge flag.

731.reading: Arriving, she saw his devotion and stood to hear him recite, and he set out his path, then the coming forth and the drawing back of things at the world's dissolution.
731.nuance: பிரளையத்து ஆக்கமும் பேர்ச்சியும, the emergence and the withdrawal, is the Sankhya cycle of manifestation and reabsorption into nature. Line 4 (ஒன்றா வகையால் உரைகளை ஒட்டா) breaks off and seems to run on into 732; its sense is not clear.
731.event: Neelakesi listens as the Sankhya teacher expounds his path and the cycle of emergence and dissolution.

claims.claim: the world comes forth from nature and is drawn back into it at dissolution

732.reading: The narrator sums up what he expounded: the supreme self, root nature and the nature that is not the root, with the rules and divisions that belong to them, the subtle matters laid down in his treatise.
732.nuance: மூலப் பகுதி and அல்லாப் பகுதி render the Sankhya distinction between primal nature and its evolutes. பாலொத்து நின்ற is obscure; it may liken the self to milk, or mean 'standing on its own side'. The supreme self (பரமாத்துமன்) returns in 746-747, where she asks how it relates to the many souls.

claims.claim: the real things are the supreme self, root nature and the evolved nature that is not the root

733.reading: He laid all this out before the gathered assembly, and she, the foremost in knowledge, questioned Parasaran as if she too longed for the truth.
733.nuance: விரும்பினள் போல, 'as though she desired it', tells the reader her questions are a debater's feint: she plays the eager pupil to draw out his doctrine before attacking it. பருங்கினன் in line 2 is an unusual form, perhaps for a verb of setting out or teaching.
733.event: Before the assembly Neelakesi questions the Sankhya teacher Parasaran, feigning a learner's eagerness.

734.reading: She asks him, as a disciple asks the one who begot her, what this teaching is; he says it is his path, she asks to be taught it, and he begins: hear these things.
734.nuance: என்னைப் பயந்தீர், 'you who gave me birth', is the address of a pupil to a teacher as spiritual parent, and continues the feint of 733; நன்னுதலாய், 'fair-browed one', is his condescending address to a woman.
734.event: Neelakesi, posing as a pupil, asks to be taught the Sankhya path, and the teacher begins.

735.reading: The Sankhya teacher lists his twenty-five categories: the abiding soul, the unmanifest, the great principle, the sense of self, the five and five senses, the one mind, the five subtle elements and the five gross elements.
735.nuance: The count works out: soul, the unmanifest (தெற்றென இல்லது, 'what is not clearly there'), மான் (mahat), செருக்கு (ahamkara), ten senses, mind, five மாத்திரை (tanmatras) and five பூதம் make twenty-five. Neelakesi pronounces these categories faulty in 739 and attacks the soul among them from 740 on.

claims.claim: reality is exhausted by twenty-five categories, from the soul and the unmanifest down to the five elements

736.reading: He describes the soul: it does nothing in any way, has none of the qualities, is a principle of its own, unstained, eternal, present everywhere, the far-seeing witness, and yet the one who experiences.
736.nuance: Line 2 (இன்பன பேதனலே பகன்) is hard to divide; அலேபகன், 'unstained', can be made out, but the rest is uncertain. The pairing in line 4 of the non-acting soul with துத்தல் உடையன், 'one who experiences or eats', is the joint Neelakesi presses in 740-745: how can what does nothing enjoy?

claims.claim: the soul does no action of any kind and is without the qualities
the soul is eternal, all-pervading, a seer and an experiencer

737.reading: He describes the unmanifest as standing, spread out and formless, with no sense organ and no action, and from it the great principle, from the sense of self the sixteen, and besides them the five elements.
737.nuance: ஈரெட்டு, 'twice eight', are the sixteen products of the sense of self (the eleven organs with mind and the five subtle elements), with the five gross elements beyond them, the classical Sankhya order of evolution. Line 1's இக்கு and line 2's division are unclear.

claims.claim: from the formless unmanifest arise the great principle, the sense of self, its sixteen products and the five elements

739.reading: Like one throwing a stone before a raging rutting elephant she declared his categories faulty, and he, swollen with pride, turned to the woman and told her to name the fault.
739.nuance: மதம் is both an elephant's rut and a school's doctrine, so மதத்தினின் மிக்கவன் is the man swollen with rut and with his creed; the simile makes her challenge brave rather than rash. உதப்பு is a rare word, taken here as the fault or flaw he demands she show.
739.event: Neelakesi declares the Sankhya categories faulty, and the angry teacher demands that she name the fault.

claims.claim: the Sankhya's twenty-five categories are faulty

740.reading: Neelakesi argues that if he says the soul does not act, then his speaking cannot be his own: these words, being the work of something else, are flawed, and the path is not even his.
740.nuance: The argument turns the doctrine on the speaker: a teacher whose self does nothing cannot claim the teaching he is uttering. Lines 1-2 (நின்னை வையாய் ... உளது அன்றெனின்) are hard to construe, and the reading of their steps is tentative.

claims.claim: if the soul does nothing, the speaker's own words are not his doing and his doctrine is not his

741.reading: She goes on: since he holds the soul does nothing in any way, even his standing as the master who teaches the principles fails, and contradiction with what is seen and falsehood cling to the doctrine.
741.nuance: Line 1 repeats 736's own words (எத்திறத்தின்னுஞ்செய்யான்) so the refutation quotes the thesis. திருட்ட விரோதம், contradiction with what is seen, is a named fault of the debate manuals: everyone sees the soul acting.

claims.claim: a soul that does nothing could not be the teacher of the principles, and the claim contradicts what is seen

742.reading: The Sankhya replies that the soul is of two kinds, and that apart from the soul that does nothing there is a soul bound up with action, from which the work of the world proceeds.
742.nuance: This is his escape from 740-741: action belongs to a karmic soul (கரும உயிர்), not to the pure one. Line 1 (பெருமை உயிர்க்குரையேன்) and the middle term in line 2 (இடை ஒன்றும்) are obscure. Neelakesi answers at once in 743.

claims.claim: there are two kinds of soul, and action comes from the soul bound with deeds

743.reading: She replies that if acting souls and non-acting souls both truly exist, his thesis is destroyed and falsehood and the other faults come upon it; what will he do now?
743.nuance: மேற்கோள் is the formal thesis of a debate; to grant an acting soul is to contradict the thesis that the soul does not act, so the defence of 742 sinks the position it defends.

claims.claim: granting acting souls beside non-acting ones destroys the thesis that the soul does not act

744.reading: She asks what an idle soul without qualities, hidden and unmanifest, actually does: if it only enjoys, how does it come to enjoy, and if everything goes on without it, what is it for?
744.nuance: சோம்பன், 'the idler', is her mocking name for the inactive soul. Line 2 (ஓம்பற்கு அருமையின் உண்ணுமாற்றான்) is hard to construe; the question 'how does it eat' answers to the experiencer of 736.

claims.claim: a soul that does nothing and without which things go on serves no purpose, and cannot be the enjoyer

745.reading: She asks how a soul that is formless and does nothing, and that on examination neither touches nor joins nature with its forms and modifications, can be the cause of its own seeing and experiencing.
745.nuance: விகிர்தி விகற்பொடு names nature's modifications and their varieties. The objection is the one she pressed against the Buddhist on how formless consciousness can be joined to a body (302); a Jain soul, of the body's size, is in contact with what it knows.

claims.claim: a soul with no action and no contact with nature cannot be the cause of seeing and experiencing

746.reading: She asks whether, if the soul stands pure, conscious, pervading everything and unchanging, nature makes it whirl in the round of births out of hatred for the released soul or love of the bound ones.
746.nuance: முத்தாத்துமன் and புத்தாத்துமாக்கள் are the released and the bound souls (புத்த for baddha, 'bound', not the Buddha). The mock alternatives, hatred or desire, are her point: a changeless pure soul gives nature no reason to bind it, so Sankhya bondage has no cause.

claims.claim: nothing could bind in the round of births a soul that is pure, pervading and changeless

747.reading: She demands that, instead of saying the supreme soul takes on the souls' modifications only as crystal takes colour from what is beside it, he state properly what the one soul is.
747.nuance: பளிங்கு அடை போல, 'like crystal by what lies near it', is the Sankhya image of a soul that only seems coloured by nature's changes. She treats the image as an evasion. மாத்திரை in line 3 may mean 'a mere measure' (only an appearance) and is uncertain.

claims.claim: the soul is only apparently modified, as crystal takes the colour of what is beside it
the crystal image explains only an appearance and does not say what the one soul is

748.reading: She closes with a dilemma: if he says the soul goes from birth to birth, his doctrine breaks; if he says it does not go, the earlier objections return; what accompanies the soul is its twofold deeds, and his speech is mere fluency of teeth and tongue.
748.nuance: Line 3 (பல்லும் நுன் நாவும் பதையாது உரை) mocks talk that runs on without the tongue faltering. எல்லும் துணையும் இருவினை is read as 'the twofold deeds are its light and companion', the Jain answer to what carries a soul between births; the line is compressed and the reading is tentative.

claims.claim: whether the soul is said to move between births or not, the Sankhya account fails
the soul's own twofold deeds accompany it through births

links.note: Both epics give the Sankhya twenty-five, but the Neelakesi counts the unmanifest and the five subtle elements while the Manimekalai counts the five sense objects and thought (சித்தம்) and leaves primal nature outside the list.
links.teaches: Two rival polemics hand down different lists under the same count of twenty-five, so the Tamil reports of Sankhya were not one fixed table and neither epic's list can stand for the school by itself.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Sankhya soul is the knowing awareness, without the three qualities, one, pervading and eternal; the Neelakesi's has the same marks but adds that it does nothing and yet experiences.
links.teaches: The Buddhist and the Jain reports agree on the soul's marks, but only the Jain report foregrounds the pair 'does nothing' and 'experiences', which is exactly the pair it then sets against each other in 740-745.

links.note: 741 quotes 736's words எத்திறத்தின்னுஞ்செய்யான் and turns them on the teacher: a soul that does nothing cannot be the master who teaches.
links.teaches: The refutation works by quotation: the Sankhya's description of the soul, repeated word for word, is shown to cancel the act of describing it.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists a thesis that goes against one's own words (சுவசன விருத்தம், 'my mother is barren') among the false theses; 743 says the Sankhya's admission of acting souls destroys his own thesis (மேற்கோள்).
links.teaches: What the Buddhist manual gives as a textbook fault with a toy example, the Jain debater springs in a live debate, showing how the logicians' catalogue of faults was used as a weapon between schools.

links.note: In 302 Neelakesi asked the Buddhist how formless consciousness could touch or be bound to a body with form; in 745 she asks the Sankhya how a formless soul with no contact with nature can see or experience.
links.teaches: One Jain objection, that the formless cannot touch the formed, is aimed at two opposite opponents, the Buddhist who denies a soul and the Sankhya who makes it untouched, which shows the Jain body-sized soul is meant as the middle that both lack.

links.note: In 307 Neelakesi answered that deeds carry the soul between births as wind turns a whirligig; in 748 she tells the Sankhya his soul, whether it goes or not, cannot be carried, and that its twofold deeds are its companion.
links.teaches: The image of deeds moving the soul that answered Mokkalan becomes the dilemma that sinks the Sankhya: only a soul that acts and is acted on can be carried by its own deeds from birth to birth.

links.note: Neelakesi asks what could bind a soul that is pure and changeless; the Tirumanthiram makes soul and bond both beginningless, so the soul was never first pure and then bound.
links.teaches: The Jain question to the Sankhya, what first bound a pure soul, is the question the Saiva verse avoids by making bondage as old as the soul, at the price of a soul that was never pure until the Lord draws near.

gains.a: The Neelakesi's question gains a known school's answer, showing that one reply to it is to deny the soul ever had a pure beginning.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's 'beginningless' gains a reason: it closes off the debating question of how a pure, unchanging soul could fall into bondage.

links.note: Kural 706 has crystal show the colour of what is near it, as the face shows the heart; the Sankhya, in Neelakesi's report, uses crystal beside a coloured thing for a soul that only seems changed.
links.teaches: The same crystal runs opposite ways: in the Kural its borrowed colour is a true sign of what lies within, in the Sankhya it is a mere appearance over a soul untouched, which is why Neelakesi can call the image an evasion.

gains.a: The Neelakesi verse gains a common Tamil use of the crystal image, in which borrowed colour reveals rather than hides, against which the Sankhya use looks like special pleading.
gains.b: The Kural couplet gains a sense of the image's other use, where crystal's colour is denied any truth, showing that its own reading of the face as a reliable sign is a choice.

links.note: The Sankhya of 735 counts twenty-five principles that need no maker; Tirumular's Lord makes the twenty-five within the womb for each birth.
links.teaches: The Saiva verse keeps the Sankhya tally of twenty-five but puts a maker over it, the one element both the Sankhya and its Jain critic do without.

gains.a: The Neelakesi list gains evidence that its twenty-five were common coin in Tamil doctrine, later taken up into a theistic account of embodiment.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's bare 'twenty-five' gains its named members and its Sankhya origin, so a reader can see what the Lord is said to assemble.

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (சாங்கிய வாதச் சருக்கம்); the id differs from vaadham, which the list already uses for alchemy

new_concepts.gloss: primal nature (prakriti) in the Sankhya: the unmanifest root from which intellect, the sense of self, the senses and the elements evolve, as against the soul
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: மூலப் பகுதி and அல்லாப் பகுதி (732); also அப்பியத்தம் (737) and விகிர்தி (745)

source_issues: Verse 738 is missing from the core file: the chapter has 18 verses for 730-748, and 739 follows 737 without a break in sense being evident.
731 line 4 (ஒன்றா வகையால் உரைகளை ஒட்டா) ends without a finite verb and seems incomplete.
733 line 2: பருங்கினன் is an unusual form, possibly corrupt.
736 line 2: இன்பன பேதனலே பகன் is hard to divide.
734 lines 1 and 3: the e-text's '•' was repaired to ஃ (இஃது, அஃது).
740 lines 1-2 and 744 line 2 are hard to construe.
